pgn：8.5 /10 评测这种类型的游戏，可以说都不可避免地需要与杀戮尖塔做对比，而这款打牌游戏在继承同类型游戏优点的同时，也确实做出了一些创新点： 1. 职业之间的团队合作 2. 引入场地的概念，有了纵深 3. 定向升级key卡的系统，减少鬼抽的挫败感 从游戏刚出的时候到现在，可以看到制作组还是有一定野心和热情的，唯一可惜的点在于，他们的产能还是太有限了。 总之喜欢打牌的话这个游戏还是不错的，如果想和朋友一起合作打牌，那么这个游戏算得上是极为推荐。

完全面向多人合作设计的卡牌，3人＞2人＞1人。数值和机制设计非常有想象力、非常放得开，虽然因此有平衡性与运气的问题，但仍然极具乐趣，加上有朋友一起就更上一层楼。视听效果模仿纸板桌游与舞台剧风格，总体不错。 与杀戮尖塔联机mod的区别？首先杀戮尖塔本身是单人游戏，联机也在各打各的，而本作有大量涉及团队互助、合作、连协的内容；其次杀戮尖塔的风格像老老实实的街头斗殴，虽然整体设定很奇幻，但没啥奇幻的味儿，左手抓凳子（防御）右手拿板砖（攻击），在被打死之前先打死对面就算赢，解题感很强。而本作则更接近DND风格，有远近距离与方向之分，有更加千奇百怪的效果与机制，仿佛与朋友组成了冒险者小队，深入地下城探险一般，乐趣会更强。

最强的流派没有之一，无尽模式无脑过，单人不带队友都可以随便打，简单并且速通。 职业：法师 核心遗物：玻璃蒺藜（这个不能少） 其它遗物：黏糊糊的手指（无限抽牌）、墨西哥卷饼（生命换法力）、其它回血的遗物，后期根本不缺。 核心卡牌：拟像（3）寒冰堡垒（配合永恒之冬快速启动格挡） 核心过牌卡：黑暗契约（1如果打伪教皇拖拉到第三回合就有用了）、编织灵脉（最好2-5张，后期拿到墨西哥卷饼后不需要那么多卡手可以移除）、神秘赌注（2张比过度好用，过度有竭力） 控制卡：永恒之冬（1）（让怪动不了，加快游戏速度。配合寒冰堡垒快速启动格挡） 队友：牧师（后面最好是一个队友都不要直接送死，这样打教皇和大魔王更简单） ban遗物：蛤蜊（这个遗物会强制拿卡，避免拿这个遗物污染卡池） 这个流派除了打伪教皇可能有点拖拉，其它BOSS都是一回合秒杀的，有些小怪会分裂，一回合有可能结束不了，但基本两回合就能结束所有战斗，包括屠夫、蝎子、石像鬼王这种限制伤害上限的，机制就是依靠拟像无限叠加格挡，很快最高就能达到32K，而玻璃蒺藜的能力就是把所有格挡转化为伤害让怪物分摊，这个伤害可以无视厨师的坚韧皮肤。

HELLCARD is one of those games that is genuinely fun right up until it suddenly isn’t. I played a decent amount of it and overall enjoyed the core gameplay loop. The art style is great, the characters are fun, and putting builds together can feel really satisfying. There were multiple runs where my group absolutely steamrolled the game; clearing 5–7 late-game floors without taking damage, beating multiple bosses on the same floor flawlessly, etc. And then the game would suddenly throw a floor at us where enemies open with 70+ damage on turn one and completely flatten the run with basically no warning. That’s the issue that kept coming back: the balance feels wildly inconsistent. It’s hard to feel motivated to keep experimenting or improving when you can have an objectively powerful build dominating the game one minute and then get instantly deleted by a random difficulty spike the next. The problem isn’t that the game is hard. The problem is that certain encounters feel disconnected from the rest of the game’s balance and pacing. I honestly think these kinds of roguelike/deckbuilder games are probably very difficult to design and tune correctly, and there’s clearly a really fun game underneath all of this. But the frustration eventually outweighs the fun. I got around 10–20 enjoyable hours out of it, but I can’t fully recommend it because the balancing issues eventually slam the brakes on what otherwise could have been a great game.

While you CAN play this solo, it shines best in a party of 2-3. This roguelike deckbuilder is designed with multiple party members in mind, whether they're controlled by one person or multiple. Takes a lot longer to play solo if you have a full party (which you probably will want to have, as it gives more options in between fights and mitigates bad draws) as you're essentially playing 3 decks at the same time. My friend recommended it to me after we had played some Slay the Spire 2 co-op, and honestly I think the co-op in this game is way more engaging. Different enemies can target different party members rather than 'BIG TANKY enemy, hits everyone'. So you can typically burst down the high damage enemies instead of having to play overly-safe blocking many rounds as you whittle down a 4x HP enemy. My biggest gripe is In-between fight progression (upgrades, card swaps/removal) is very rng heavy, especially if you aren't rolling in cash, and it's something I hope they alter/change in the sequel. The game also heavily favours thin decks with a few strong cards, though it's not the only viable playstyle. As it stands though, a decent deckbuilder that only improves whilst playing co-op.

MUSIC sound is terrible and here is WHY! [always mute it, as I do not like to torture myslef] Short-loop fatigue – probably the closest informal term in game audio circles. A music loop is so short that repetition becomes obvious very quickly. Repetitive ostinato – if the music is built around the same repeating rhythmic or melodic figure (an ostinato). Most songs create expectation through: - verse → chorus, - tension → release, - harmonic progression, - changing instrumentation, - larger-scale structure. A 10–30 second game loop often restarts before any of those expectations can build. Instead of feeling like a complete musical phrase, your brain notices the restart itself. Once you recognize the loop boundary, it becomes difficult to ignore, which accelerates annoyance. Game audio designers often avoid this by using: - long loops (2–5+ minutes), - layered adaptive music that changes with gameplay, - horizontal resequencing (different musical segments played in varying orders), - vertical remixing (adding/removing instrument layers instead of restarting the track). And for the LOVE of GOD make better music. Reaching the Archdemon's Hell level finally made the title click. The real torture isn't the enemies—it's realizing you've been listening to the same 20-second music loop for the entire run. Maybe the real title is HELLSONG. You are welcome. [h1]HELLCARD: A Fantastic Co-op Deckbuilder with a Few Frustrating Rough Edges[/h1] [i]HELLCARD surprised me more than I expected. I came for the deckbuilding, stayed for the co-op, and ended up having far more fun than I thought I would. While it's absolutely enjoyable solo, I genuinely think this game shines brightest when played with friends. Every run turns into a mix of planning, chaos, and laughing when everything inevitably goes wrong.[/i] [h2]🤝 One of the Most Enjoyable Co-op Deckbuilders I've Played[/h2] The biggest strength of HELLCARD is easily its cooperative gameplay. Every player brings a completely different class to the party, and they don't just feel like different colors with slightly different cards—they genuinely play differently. Finding combinations that work together is incredibly satisfying, and coordinating turns with friends makes every battle feel more strategic than in most deckbuilders. Personally, I always enjoyed playing the Mage the most. Filling my deck with powerful Bolt spells and watching everything explode never stopped being fun. [h2]🃏 Simple to Learn, Hard to Master[/h2] Every run encourages experimentation. You'll constantly discover new cards, relics, and combinations that completely change how your deck plays. Even after several runs, I was still finding builds I hadn't considered before. Because every class approaches combat differently, trying another character almost feels like learning a completely new game. [h2]⚠️ Drawbacks[/h2] Not every room feels worth entering. Some encounters require Gems that are often too limited to justify spending, making those rooms easy to skip. Even more frustrating are rooms filled with large numbers of summoning enemies. Especially in multiplayer, it can feel like someone unknowingly picked the "wrong" path, only for the whole team to spend several minutes clearing endless waves of summoned creatures. Those fights usually aren't difficult—they just drag on much longer than they need to. The recent German localization is unfortunately another weak point. Some translations feel awkward or simply incorrect compared to earlier versions. If you don't mind playing in English, I'd honestly recommend doing so. [h2]🏆 Conclusion[/h2] HELLCARD offers a unique take on the roguelike deckbuilder genre, and its cooperative gameplay alone makes it stand out from most similar games. Despite a few repetitive encounters and some questionable translation changes, I kept coming back because every run felt different, every class had its own identity, and playing with friends was simply a lot of fun. If you enjoy games like Slay the Spire but wish you could experience that style of gameplay together with friends, HELLCARD is definitely worth checking out. [h3]Rating: 8/10[/h3]
